Well, now in this question of jazz and defining it, don't you think one of the problems that not only critics, but anyone who's discussing the art form has, is that jazz flourished, I guess you could say, in New Orleans for a period of, what, 20 years or something like that. And then all of a sudden it, you know, by 1920, things began to change, at least as the music carried itself outside of New Orleans. And it went through different, I guess you would term different stylistic changes. I mean, the form remained, but there were stylistic changes.

The form remained, the style changed, and when the style did change, its normal process of change was rarely, if ever, based on fundamental aesthetic developments. But usually, and I would say possibly invariably, on social and economic ground. So that the concept, for instance, of Chicago jazz, I use words like that in quotes, but Chicago jazz did not come about because somebody ever had a new idea. But it came about because of the fact that it was forced to come about by historical circumstances. For instance, at the time when the musicians left New Orleans, and of course when they left New Orleans, they left because they couldn't make any money here anymore. When they left New Orleans, they went up the river, and arrived in Chicago, which happens to be the closest major upper river port, where there were people and entertainment going on. They arrived precisely at the beginning of the Prohibition era. And in a period when the gangsters had not yet made their arrangements with the police. So the jobs were available almost exclusively in speakeasies. Now, the speakeasy, of course, is a clandestine place which was not supposed to be selling liquor, and people would come and knock on the door, you know, and it was a kind of a secret operation. And it really was a secret operation in the beginning. Now, it was immediately apparent that you couldn't have a jazz band with a trumpet playing in a basement somewhere because any policeman could hear it passing in the street. So, therefore, in the early stages, the trumpet players were eliminated from the bands entirely. And the premium, then, was on the clarinet playing the lead in a soft tone and playing solos, which was fundamentally, as an extended form, an entirely new concept to these musicians. It was not the kind of thing that they had done in the past. And so, the clarinet player started to play melody rather than harmony, which is his historic role. And that stylistic change then takes place because of the pressures of society. It has nothing to do with the sudden inspiration on the part of the performer. Jimmy Noon is a good illustration of this. And the re-instrumentation of the jazz band as exemplified in the Apex Club Orchestra, which you can refer to on records, is a good illustration of what happened.

It would be fair to say that due to economic, social, political circumstances, that jazz went through various changes in forms from, let's say, what I'm familiarly, what I primarily call traditional jazz or New Orleans jazz, went through changes to, let's say, in the mid-30s swing, and then up through bebop or bop style, and then the so-called progressive jazz, all these different styles, due to various changes in the social structure. In the first place, in the first place, your general pursuit of this matter reflects certain glaring prejudices, which it is necessary to deal with because they are not exclusively yours. And that is mostly marked by your discussion based on the black man coming north, you see, which is, as far as a jazz form is concerned, a total irrelevancy. Well, wasn't jazz primarily the music of the black American? Of course not. And not only that, but in the process of the coming north, there were quite as many white musicians, possibly more white musicians, involved in the northern trek than black musicians. They were all jazz musicians. They were all faced with identical problems in performance and recognition. The jazz music was not a primarily black form. The jazz music was a product, as I said in a book, of a place and not a race. The phenomenon occurred in New Orleans and, in my opinion, could not have occurred anywhere else. Did not occur here because there were blacks here. That is not to say that blacks didn't make their contribution to the music. They certainly did. But they didn't make their contribution because they were blacks. They made their contribution because they were part of the scene and the music was being produced here. Now, of course, because of definitive failures, that is, failures in definition that are common in the discussions of jazz, people that deal with it, for the most part, have not yet learned to make the distinctions between the many forms of music that in fact took place. There is, for instance, the blues, which is clearly a black form. The assumption that the blues was fundamental to the development of jazz is false. It certainly didn't hurt having it around, did it? No, it didn't hurt having it around, just as it didn't hurt to have any kind of music around, just as the operatic areas that were performed in the French opera found their way into jazz performance, as did the old French quadrilles, which are far more represented in what we think of as the standard jazz material than the blues. And as a matter of fact, in dealing with the blues form as such, New Orleans was fundamentally hostile to the blues. All right. Now, can you just elaborate upon this a little bit? I don't want you to go through... I'm fairly familiar with Marxian philosophy myself.
Mm-hmm.
But, well, I know that you also mentioned that in relation to jazz that you were very interested in the musical form of jazz, that you didn't care that much about the musicians.
Mm-hmm.
That you were just interested in the music. Now, I'm going to ask kind of a pedestrian question, but do you see yourself as a humanist?
No. Not at all.
All right. Why not?
Well, it's...
Marx was a humanist as far as I'm concerned.

Well, I think you'd be doing him an injustice. Actually, I don't think that he was a humanist. As a matter of fact, the concept of humanism carries with it certain mystical connotations, which, to my way of thinking, don't really have anything to do with logical thinking. And...
So you don't think that Marx's utopian ushering in the millennium is...
Oh, certainly not. It's not a... Far from that.
It's not a mystical way of looking at things?

Certainly not. No, I think that the way we're doing it now is a mystical way of doing it. I think that the concept of capitalism in its current stage of decay is a completely unrealistic and utopian dream, which we are viewing in a given stage of its collapse.
Well, what... How much does your... How would you relate your social and political philosophy to your views of the music, for instance?

Well, only to the extent that... Gee, I hate to go into this because of the fact that it's going to take such an enormous lot of time to do. Okay, well, let's... The... I consider certain artistic manifestations to be what I would consider to be socially useful. And, in other words, healthy.
Okay, okay. That might be where the Marx thing comes in.
Right.
And that they rise out of the economic circumstances.
That's right.
Yeah. But now, if you're an economic determinist, it must mean you believe that once... The economics...
because it has to determine everything.
Yes, I do believe that.
It determines social, political, artistic.
Right.
Artistic. So there's no, you don't believe there's any emotional value whatsoever to jazz music?
Oh, there's enormous emotional value to it. And there's a humanistic value to it? My responses to it are visceral responses.
Well, then doesn't that contradict your attitude that you're not a humanist?
No, not at all. I'm not saying that I am a man that lives without an emotional life because I don't and no man is. That's not involved in it at all.
But you did say you didn't have any stake in the emotional lives of the musicians.

That's right. And I really believe that the level of a man's civilization can be best determined by the extent to which he is able to achieve a point where his brain guides his emotions. Instead of vice versa.
Yeah.

And when I see the individual problems of not only musicians but people, it's very difficult for me to think of them in terms of the individual musician. I see it as a general social problem of which he is a part. I say to myself, you know, by talking to this man, I'm not going to solve this problem because his problem is a universal problem. And he's going to have to swim upstream, that's all, in order to cope with it.
Do you think Karl Marx would have endorsed jazz as a music of the proletariat?
I don't think he would ever have gotten close enough to hear it. I don't think he would have taken the time to listen.
Would you use the word proletariat in regards to music?
No. I wouldn't.
In other words, you don't take the view as an orthodox Marxist that there's some class structure?
That jazz is a people's music?
Or that there's a... What class does it represent? I don't think it represents a class.

I think that it represents a... What it actually represents is a reflection of a given society in a very schematic setting, which had its delights, just as Xanadu does for the literarian. But it's outgrown its usefulness. I think its usefulness would prevail, provided that a setting existed for it. But it just happens that it's a play without a stage.
But no music can survive unless it's socially and economically useful. That's right.
Or has.
But it also exists as an aesthetic form, which is separate from the social... Of course. ...separate from the social, which has emotional value and aesthetic value.
That's right.

Of course. You may be more of a humanist than you think. I don't know. Oh, another thing I wanted to ask you, Al, was that something came up in the interview, which said you were also a member of the Mensa.
Yes. Now... I was. I haven't been paying dues lately.
All right. Now, what is the purpose of this organization?
Of Mensa? Yeah.
Could you just briefly...
Well, Mensa is an organization that is dedicated to... Well, actually, what it is, is an organization of people whose IQs are in the first 1% of the population.
Mm-hmm.
But at the time when I became involved in it, its principal activities had to do with the identification at early ages of gifted children and the development of educational programs for them.
Mm-hmm.

So that's what it was. But on my own application to the thing, I began to consider that the whole testing process was worthless and that you cannot, in fact, identify gifted children if there is such a thing. And certainly that trying to reorganize educational programs under the social structure in which we live is a hopeless job.
Mm-hmm.
So I'm a dropout from Mensa. My wife continues her membership, and my kids do, but I don't.
But the purpose of it is to instigate certain social programs?
No, no, not at all. As a matter of fact, it's...
Or is it to just exist to...

Theoretically, it's supposed to exist as a meeting ground for people who can communicate with each other, who have difficulty communicating with other people because their intelligences are too highly developed, which, of course, that is the conception. I no longer agree with the whole idea. Mm-hmm. Or even the fact that you can establish... Or the fact that IQs have any meaning. I don't believe in it. Hmm.
But you remember this from an early age?

Well, I remember it for quite a while. It didn't start until 1946. Oh, I see. But I had an interest in it because of my own early career, which had to do with the fact that I had the highest IQ score in the nation on the original college... When they first instituted the college IQ testing for a freshman the first year, I had the highest IQ in the nation. And the Roosevelt administration, at that time, through its brain trust with Raymond Moley and Rexford Guy Tugwell, came up with this crackpot program of picking out the most intelligent kids and bringing them to Washington and doing a big thing. So I got to know the president, Mrs. Roosevelt, and I became close friends with Eleanor Roosevelt and spent a lot of time with her in my early days. And I had the opportunity to meet people that I wanted to discuss certain things with. And the government made it possible for me to interview Albert Einstein and John Dewey. And this is how I met Rivera, too.
Mm-hmm. That's how you met Rivera.
Yeah.

Yeah. Maybe, maybe, I think what I want to ask you now is that you've, throughout the interview, you've been mentioning certain musicians that you knew, and you could list more that you knew quite well. And I think that it might be a good idea now to get some idea of how you had access to all these musicians. In other words, you were in the business of producing concerts, I take it right?
Yes.

And I think that your knowledge of jazz, your interest in jazz, and your knowing musicians relates to this. And could you just brief us a little bit on your, on your, one of your occupations as a producer? You were involved in certain concert productions.
Well, my, my, I think we get, I think. You got time. I think. Oh, no, you're right.

This is real for Al. Okay. When we were talking about Big Spider-Beck, Miles Davis came up, and it was pretty apparent from the way you're talking that you knew him. Yeah. In some capacity, personally. Now, you know some, you know quite a few musicians, personally. How do you know these guys so personally?

Do you just go up to them and say hi and get to know them, or what? No, I don't think I ever did that. As a matter of fact, I can't really say that I was ever especially interested in getting to know musicians at all, as, as musicians, as people. Okay, all right. But my, my own activity, besides the ones that I just knew socially from around New Orleans.
Yeah.

You see. Because you lived here. Because I lived here. But in getting out of town, when I went to college, I went to Temple University in Philadelphia. Mm-hmm. And at that time, I came with an enormous collection of phonograph records, because I couldn't really see myself surviving through the period of a college education without the music. So I had this large collection of records. Now, it happened that, that this was a time of a reawakening of an interest in American popular music, especially among people who were interested in swing.
Mm-hmm.

But even among these people, there was a consciousness of the personalities and the people that had recorded the early jazz. Some of those people, of course, were playing in swing bands. And the fact that I had this collection became very well known in school, and people used to come to my room all the time to listen to records. And to discuss with me the music that they were playing, and they were much interested in this. Well, in 1935, the American Newspaper Guild was about to, was planning an annual affair. They have a, like a, a ball, you see. And a young man who was then the radio editor of the Philadelphia Evening Bulletin, whose name was Park Breck, got the idea that it would be a good thing to have a New Orleans jazz concert. And he knew somebody who knew me. So they came to me and asked me if I knew of any way that it would be possible to put together a concert of authentic New Orleans jazz in Philadelphia. And the question then was, from my standpoint, who was in the neighborhood? And the, the guild was prepared to foot the bill for it. So, uh, after discussion, uh, since they were going to have a dance anyway, in addition to this, and these were to take place on different floors of the building, with a dance on the third floor and a jazz concert on the second floor, I proposed that the newly organized band of Jack Teagarden would be, uh, attractive to, to bring in. It was a band that didn't last very long, but it was fortunate enough to have, uh, people like Sterling Bose and Irving Fazola in the band. And then, uh, because of various grapevine considerations, I, I learned who was in New York among the musicians. And I got hold of Sidney Bechet and Sidney D. Paris and Freddie Moore, the drummer known as Gate Mouth Moore.
Now, had you done any of this kind of thing before?
No.
Well, how, how did, how did it occur to you that you could get a hold of Sidney Bechet, for instance?
Well, I knew he was in New York.
Okay. But, I mean, you, you never were before, uh, in the role of doing this kind of thing, talking to musicians.
No, this was, this was my first experience with dealing with him. How about in New Orleans?
And you, you never had that kind of relationship with the musicians here, promoting their music?
No, there was nothing to promote. I mean, you, there was no, uh, uh, see, there was no such thing as a concept of a jazz concert.
Yeah.

It didn't exist. Okay. So, I called, uh, I called Bechet and I, and he suggested Sidney D. Paris and, and Gate Mouth. And, uh, so I just made a deal with him to bring him in. And, in fact, it was Sidney who taught me the procedure. He says, well, you send us the tickets. Uh, and as soon as we get the tickets, we'll consider that a firm commitment and we'll come in, you see. So, we set the time and, uh, I got some local musicians that I already knew from Philadelphia. And so, uh, everything came together. And in 1936, in the beginning of 1936, we had, uh, the jazz concert where tickets were sold for people to come in and sit down and listen to music. And, uh, uh, uh, then I invited musicians from the dance band upstairs to come down to participate. And so, we did have Jack T. Garden and Bose and Fazola. And, uh, the combination of all these musicians made, uh, really an excellent concert.
Mm-hmm.

And, uh, the people were extremely enthusiastic and they didn't get out of the concert until two o'clock the next afternoon. In broad daylight. The next afternoon. That's right. Mm-hmm. We started at eight o'clock at night and kept on until two o'clock the next afternoon, which may also be a marathon record for jazz concerts. So, anyway, uh, after that, uh, I was widely congratulated and people, uh, were saying, well, you know, we gotta do this again. And then I took to, uh, to, uh, hiring small halls, uh, for small groups of people and, and arranging with the musicians to come in and play. Then I was approached by, uh, the radio station there, WFIL, uh, which was the ABC affiliate at the time. And they asked me if I would come in and do a regular record show, uh, based on this kind of music. And, uh, I did, entitled Journeys into Jazz, uh, which still runs on tape in various parts of the country at various times. And, uh, so, uh, people began to identify me with the music. And having done so, of course, the musicians that I was associated with then would let me know what was happening and who was available and because jobs were scarce in those days. Now, it also happened that the university was right across the street from a theater, which was called Nixon's Grand Theater, where most of the, uh, black musical attractions played. And so, uh, and of course, a lot of the members of those bands were New Orleans musicians, some of whom I knew from New Orleans. And some of whom, uh, uh, were referred to me by other people, by other musicians.
Uh-huh.

You see, in New York. Who knew them? So I used to take to going across the street whenever a new band came in and saying hello and finding out who was going to be doing what and if there was a possibility I might be able to use them on a concert.
Uh-huh.

And, uh, this is how I met people like Danny Barker, for instance. Uh-huh. Even though I had seen him performing in New Orleans when I was a kid, I didn't know his name and I didn't identify the name with the person until I met him in backstage at Nixon's Grand and Red Allen and people like that.
Did you have, in producing these concerts, did you have a stake more in the New Orleans musicians than you did in others?
I wasn't really making the distinction yet myself. I was interested in good jazz musicians, and I used a lot of good Chicago and New York musicians.
In other words, you hadn't come to your narrow definition of jazz yet.

That's right. And, for example, many times people worked for me, like Mesro and Pee Wee Russell and Miff Mole and Joe Sullivan. This was all jazz to you? All jazz to me. Still is all jazz. It is? Yes. But anyway, I came to know all these people. Art Hodes used to come and work for me frequently. And it eventually came to a point where I was identified with jazz in Philadelphia, so that nobody even thought of doing anything with jazz in Philadelphia without calling me first.
I see. Now, let me ask you this. What year did you first do this? 1936?
That was in 1936, yeah.
Were you a student at Temple then?
Mm-hmm.
You were an undergraduate.
Yeah.
Now, do you have to have a business sense? I mean, is this a real business, entrepreneurial type of thing?
Well, it could be, but it wasn't for me, because all I was interested in doing was bringing the music together and listening to it myself.
But, I mean, to get a concert hall and to get, I mean, all those mechanical things, how the hell did you ever get that?
Well, I'm a very resourceful guy.
Yeah.
I mean, I think of what needs to be done, and I just know that there's a way to do it, and I just go and do it. And I've always done that.
But originally, you were the first, you were approached by somebody who was interested in the idea.
That's right.
Yeah. So that was a help.
Yes, it was. It wouldn't have occurred to me otherwise.
Right.

And then I just, in the process of this, you see, when you're already identified with an area like jazz, you see, especially even in those days, other people didn't make the distinctions. For example, I'd be approached by somebody to participate with him in the production of a concert, which was not necessarily music that I was interested in.
Mm-hmm.

And I was always prepared to discuss. I mean, I even collaborated in the production of a Duke Ellington concert one time with Rhys Dupree, who was the composer of Shorten and Bread, was the co-producer who talked me into it, and who also was the one who introduced me to Jelly Roll Morton. Mm-hmm.
Was it the year that the Goodman band?
Yes, that was the same year as the Goodman band?
It wasn't any relationship.
No, no. That was John Hammond's production.
I was going to ask you about John Hammond.
Yes.
Because he seemed to also have the concert idea.
Was that the concert idea of producing jazz? Yes, that was a swing production. Those were common.
They were?
Yeah, I mean, that was being done anyway.
Earlier than 1936?

Yes, earlier than the Carnegie Hall thing. But I was bringing real jazz men into Carnegie Hall. And to Symphony Hall in Boston. Mm-hmm. And I did a concert in Hollywood Bowl. And in general, had some...
Who did you bring to Carnegie Hall?

Carnegie Hall. That was Muggsy Spanier, Sidney Bechet, Joe Sullivan, Pops Foster, Baby Dodds. The same group that I brought on my Ivy League tour when we toured the Ivy League schools. You know, showing jazz to the music departments where I would do a little lecture and illustrate it with music.
Who... Now, when you were approached at Temple to do a concert, why were you approached?
Well, because I was the only one who knew anything about it. I had a collection of records, for example, that everybody knew.
Oh, I see.
You see. I see. And besides that, it was known that I was from New Orleans.
When did you start collecting the records? Or did you get them from your...
I always had them. I just don't know. I just don't...
I'm wondering if you mentioned your uncle had always collected them or something.
Yeah. Or did it come down through your family? Yes, of course. Another thing is that I knew musicians...
You took them to Temple with you?
Yeah, sure.
Oh, those 78s?

That's right. Yeah. Because, well, there was nothing else to take. And all those... See, there are a lot of musicians that the family just hired from time to time, like to go out to Millenburg for a picnic. I mean, we'd hire Papa Celestan's band, you know. And so I knew all the musicians. I've known, for example, Jeanette Kimball, who plays the piano in Papa Celestan's band. I've known her since I was five years old. And so, you know, having grown up with a musician like that, I mean, a musician was never anything exotic to me.
Mm-hmm.
You see?

It seems to me that, you know, in a sense, you're in a class of people. And I put Hammond in with you, to a certain extent, you may disagree with me. But these people, like yourself and Hammond, that started producing jazz concerts, were also interested in record collecting. Or maybe, you know, or at least had a lot of records.
Usually.
The phenomenon of record collecting here seems to be very important.
Well, in the first place, you have to be interested in some kind of music.
Yeah.
And, uh...
Or preserving, too, a certain kind of music.
Well, I don't think that ever occurred to me in those days, because it never occurred to me that it was in danger.
Yeah.

But, uh, I don't, I never thought of there being anything to preserve yet, you see? There was no reason to think in those terms. And besides that, I hadn't done yet a lot of the theoretical thinking that I have done since, which is understandable. But, uh, uh, I think that the first thing that's necessary is that you feel a need for the music. And then you feel a need to share the music with other people who are interested in what you've got, you see? And you realize that they don't have the opportunity to listen. And, of course, in those days, we didn't have any such thing as tape recorders, that you'd be able to run off items from your collection for other people. So, but other people wanted to hear the music, you see? So I just, uh, got concerts together, really, for them.
Uh-huh.
And, of course, there were enough of them at the time to fill the houses.
Uh-huh.

And then when I would go someplace like Chicago or St. Louis, I would work with whoever was the disc jockey that had the jazz audience. And we would co-produce, like Dave Garroway in Chicago or Rush Hughes in St. Louis, that kind of thing. And I worked out a little route, you know, for jazz bands. Uh-huh. And everybody has worked for me. Uh-huh. And there was also even a time when I had a foray into bebop, because there were so many, uh, of the people who were interested in the music that I was producing, that started to talk to me about doing some of the new stuff. And giving the people an opportunity to hear that, because they didn't have any chance to hear that in Philadelphia.
Uh-huh.

And, uh, the first concert I brought in, in fact, uh, for them, in fact, the only time when I actually ever produced a bebop concert, which I did not produce under my own name, but which featured Lenny Tristano and Fats Navarro and, uh, Billy Bauer and, uh, certain other musicians whose activity was, uh, significant at that time. Uh, you asked about Miles Davis before. Uh-huh. I met Miles Davis in Philadelphia, too. And I met him, uh, there was a, a fellow by the name of Nat Siegel, who was a small, he owned a club called the Downbeat, where these musicians got together and met. And, uh, he invited me over there one time to discuss a major concert, which would include both their kind of music and my kind of music. And Miles Davis was playing in his place that night. And that was the first time that I met him. And, uh, I, as a matter of fact, I had never heard of him before. Uh, I didn't even know what instrument he played. And when, when I sat down at the table with Nat, I didn't even know that he was one of the musicians. But we talked for a while. And then, uh, after having talked for a while, he got up and he played. And I realized that what he was playing was nothing that I could, could produce for my audience.
Mm-hmm.

And I wasn't sure that I wanted, at that time, I wasn't sure that I wanted any identification with it at all. But I was interested to hear what he was doing. And, uh, so when he came back to the table, I talked to him about it again. And, uh, I asked him some questions because I was genuinely curious to know what had led him into this strange approach to music. And I found him to be, uh, literally unable to express himself, uh, verbally. And, uh, uh, after that, I met him other times, you know, because when you're around with musicians, other musicians come in. Uh, I met him a couple of times in Birdland. And I met him in Minton's. Mm-hmm. And I met him, uh, in the Village Vanguard.
Mm-hmm.
And, uh, so when you say hello, you know.
Do you think he's a great musician?
Oh, no. I don't think that he is of really any musical consequence at all.

Mm-hmm. You have some fairly, uh, well, I shouldn't, I don't know whether unorthodox or what, but, uh, views on some musicians. Uh, for instance, uh, there's probably no doubt in most people's minds that they're interested in jazz if they agree with all the people that are supposed to know something about it, that Duke Ellington is one of the great, great American, uh, music makers.
Yeah, well, that's a great American myth.
You have a completely different view of Duke Ellington.
That's true, huh?
Can you just explain a little bit?
Yeah, well.
I think it's interesting.

Well, I think that it's interesting. I think that it's interesting that Duke Ellington has developed the reputation that he has. Uh, really, uh, uh, uh, that he has accepted as being a great musical genius. Uh, one thing is, of course, that so far as I am able to determine on the basis of what I considered to be reasonable investigation. First, that he was not, in fact, a composer, that he never really composed anything at all of any significance, certainly none of the things with which his name is identified. That we already know who was responsible for the successful things. We know, here in New Orleans, certainly we know that Lorenzo Teo wrote Mood Indigo some eight years before...
Jimmy Noon's soul became the Creole Love Call. Jimmy Noon's solo in one of the King Oliver pieces.
That's right, became the Creole Love Call. The sophisticated lady, of course, lock, stock, and barrel as Otto Hardwicks. The arrangements were made by...
But isn't, Al, let me ask you this, isn't that the definition of a jazz composer to a certain extent, that he does draw upon his musicians in a way?

Well, it's not a question of drawing upon his musicians. It's the fact that he has literally used their material, you see, and the music is published with their names on it. It is not as though Ellington removed their identification. No, I mean, the point is that it says, sophisticated lady, Otto Hardwick and Duke Ellington. Unfortunately, I mean, it's not unethical for Ellington to have his name on it. That's not what I'm suggesting. Okay. Or that his name appears with Barney Begard's on Mood Indigo, which Barney Begard had nothing to do with the composition of that either. Take the A train, says Hodges, Ellington. This is all true. But what I'm saying is that in none of these cases did Ellington make any contribution to the composition. These were all compositions of these various people. Now, because of slick publicity, he has been presented as a great creative genius who has composed all these pieces. But it's not just slick publicity, you know.
It's people like Gunther Schuller, who in their book, Early Jazz, call him the first great composer.

Well, they need to have done a little more investigating than they did. But apparently, he doesn't know what actually took place in these things. And if he were to investigate it, even superficially, he would find that these things are true.
Now, didn't he write a lot of songs, though?
Who, Ellington?
Yeah.
None that I'm able to discover that he actually wrote. Or even that he actually contributed to.
So what did he do?
Well, what he did was to present the material to audiences, which he did very well.
Did he? How? What do you mean?
Well, I mean, he could sit at a piano and smile. And he could get up on a microphone and make comments that were pleasing to people.

Wasn't he good at drawing out the best in his musicians? For instance, many of whom were New Orleans musicians. Wasn't he talented in the way he placed them and in the way in which he brought them out to their forms?

I don't think so. I don't think he contributed to that. I think that whoever happened to be functioning as concertmaster and as man, and I think that whoever happened to be doing the arrangements were the people who were responsible for that. And he did have great people. You see, there's no question about that. But the fact that he had great people does not make him a great composer. He was certainly not a great musician. I think even his closest associates would agree to that. And that his major contribution was his inability to front a band. However, this is not what he's famous for. He's famous for things that he couldn't do. And I consider that sad commentary on the general public and its willingness to accept. And even the critics like Gunther Schuller and so on who make statements like that without a genuine understanding of what happened.
Well, of course, Gunther Schuller wrote a whole book on musical development.
Yeah, I try to forget it.
Okay. Let me ask you about another jazz great who's a particularly...
and that's Charlie Parker. I know that you've had dealings with him in your own recording industry to a certain extent at work. But would you say that Charlie Parker's a great musician?

No. I would say that Charlie Parker was a musician who developed high skills in doing particular things that were of interest to him. But I wouldn't say that he was a great musician, certainly not that. I would say that his music is, of course, largely influenced by Rudy Valli, according to...
This is something I don't quite understand.
I would have to refer you to Charlie Parker himself on that subject, and he expanded it considerably in Downbeat. So if you look in the Downbeat Index, you'll find Charlie Parker himself.
Did he say he likes Rudy Valli?
No, he says that he did everything he could to make it possible for himself to sound like...
But jazz musicians are always notorious. Like Fats Waller plays... I said he played organ and he liked some organ player.
He did like...
Who was the most smelty organ player in the world. And there was no way by listening to Fats Waller's music that you were going to say that he was influenced by that organ.

Well, what I am saying is that if you listen to Rudy Valli, and especially to Dick Stabile on records, and if you listen to them... You're going to hear all those fast changes that Parker makes? You're going to hear all those things that Parker makes. I don't believe it. Well, try it and see. I don't believe that. I recommend that you try it and see, because it'll be illuminating for you to do that. And I considered that Charlie Parker was very pleasant. He had a tendency to be narcissistic. He was friendly but unresponsive to people around him. He smiled a lot. He was very cooperative, certainly. And I considered him to be a pleasant personality. The music that he played never did interest me at all. And what he did mainly was to play with the medium. And I believe that it's necessary for somebody to do more than that in order to be a great artist. That is, that unless the artist is expressing his own reactions to the world and to the society in which he lives, in his medium, that his stuff can only then be of value as exercises.
I hear a lot of protest in Charlie Parker.
Yeah, of course. I hear protest too, but I believe that it's unfocused.
He apparently was very conscious of the racial question.

Well, that's what I kept hearing all the time, but it never seemed to manifest itself in actual relationships. As a matter of fact, I considered that there was less of that in Charlie's personality than in most of the musicians that I know. He was perfectly prepared to take any individual on his face value, regardless of his color. And I don't think that he felt oppressed by being black. Certainly no more than other musicians have. I know black musicians who, for instance, won't eat fried chicken or watermelon in public because they are self-conscious about the black image. You see? And of course, I deplore this circumstance. I deplore the image and I deplore their self-consciousness about it. But Parker didn't seem to have that kind of attitude toward things. He really seemed to be prepared to do anything he wanted to do. And he seemed extremely relaxed and easy.
Are there any musicians that do not relate so much to the New Orleans style that you are particularly impressed by or with?

Yeah, of course, I was much impressed with Lips Page, whom I consider to be a great individual artist. I was impressed with Lucky Roberts, who's, I suppose, not only because of his music, but because of the environment of that place and that time. I was, of course, impressed with Pee Wee Russell, whom I was very fond of personally. That's a guy that I always enjoyed having around. And, of course, these are not New Orleans folks. I like, there were a lot of musicians that I liked personally whose music I didn't like at all, which is even more common.
